legal cornice ceiling 17.55 m for a 18.00 m street; built to 16.85 m (96% of it) — the law says how tall you may build, programme and money say how tall you did.
  · era second_empire (Règlement du 27 juillet 1859)
  · street width 18.00 m -> legal cornice ceiling 17.55 m (Règlement du 27 juillet 1859)
  · roof envelope diagonal_45: ridge 3.20 m above the cornice (legal max 3.20 m)
  · garret storeys: a second storey of chambres de bonne costs 2.90 m of the 17.55 m legal cornice, which would leave 14.65 m of stone under it — less than the 14.81 m a trade floor, its entresol and three letting storeys need. The servants in the roof are the servants of the households below, and there would not be enough of them
  · class comfortable: facade ambition 0.96 (INFERRED, only the ordering is contractual) -> facade target 16.85 m (96% of the 17.55 m the stone face may fill)
  · entrance: a 18.00 m street admits a carriage (INFERRED — a carriage must draw out of the traffic and turn in off the roadway to use a porte cochère; on a narrower street the gateway leads to a cour nothing could reach) and a comfortable household keeps one, so the entrance is a porte cochère (3.40 m of frontage, ABSOLUTE)
  · ground floor (shop): 3.95 m (SOURCED — Daly 1864 (Sér. 1 Vol. 1 t. 2), rez-de-chaussée floor-to-floor over 16 buildings: median 3.95 m, range 3.42-4.85 m, class medians 4.20 / 3.95 / 3.81 m. The ladder falls 9 % across the whole social range while the ranges overlap almost completely, so the commercial ground storey is ABSOLUTE and class-independent (scale-bar measured, ±10 %, with the 125 Champs-Élysées printed ladder anchoring the Première end))
  · storey minimum 2.60 m (Règlement du 27 juillet 1859)
  · typical storey band [2.60, 3.23, 3.69] m: a plain storey of 2.60 m (a room a person lives in, plus the floor structure carrying the one above) plus the margin ambition buys above it — class comfortable scales the MARGIN only, never the plain storey inside it
  · entresol: ground floor (shop) wants an entresol and class comfortable will pay for it: 2 letting storey(s) still stand over it inside a 16.85 m facade budget (needs 13.48 m). Decided from programme, before the budget is filled — never from what the budget left over
  · entresol height 3.06 m (SOURCED — Daly 1864 (Sér. 1 Vol. 1 t. 2): nine Deuxième Classe entresols, entresol/ground ratio median 0.775 (range 0.585-0.871), heights 2.40-3.12 m about a median of 2.98 m (scale-bar measured, ±10 %). Applied to this building's 3.95 m ground storey. ABSOLUTE, because an ABSOLUTE ground storey times a ratio is ABSOLUTE: the entresol is the top of the shop's own volume and does not move with ambition — its PRESENCE is the class marker, not its height) — reserved as a fixed element of the vertical run, immediately over the ground floor
  · facade target 16.85 m rounded to 16.85 m — the height a whole-storey stack can actually fill over 7.01 m of fixed slot(s), capped by the 17.55 m legal ceiling. The fraction is a target, not a quota, and a section is built of whole storeys
  · [vertical] budget 16.8480 m
  · [vertical] 2 fixed slot(s) reserve 7.0113 m at exactly their preferred width — absolute, so they never absorb
  · [vertical] 3 bay(s) at preferred 3.2325 m, centreline to centreline = 9.6975 m
  · [vertical] slack +0.1392 m
  · [vertical] widened the filler in each bay by 0.0464 m (0.1392 m absorbed)
  · [vertical] rung WIDEN_FILLER; residual 0.000e+00 m
  · taper: 3 typical storey(s) at rate 0.93 (INFERRED), held inside [2.60, 3.69] m -> [3.604, 3.351, 3.117] m, bottom to top
  · squeezed storey held down to 2.83 m: Daly's fraction of the 3.95 m ground storey is 3.06 m, which is not short of the 3.60 m letting storeys this section stands over it — a low storey over a shop is low relative to the floor it serves, and Daly measures that floor at 1.275× it (1.25 in Première Classe, 1.30 in Deuxième). The 0.23 m it gives up stands in the letting storeys over it, which is the floor the relation is about (A16.2): the facade was granted this budget and fills it, and the only height a facade loses is height nobody could use
  · comble CEILING 3.90 m over the 16.85 m eaves it springs from — the égout du toit, where the decree springs it, not the legal cornice: the gabarit's top is 20.75 m above the pavement (17.55 m legal cornice + 3.20 m comble), and the 0.70 m of cornice height this facade declined to build is legal height the roof still has over it — not height the roof forfeited with it. The same curve is simply traced to a taller top, which costs 3.90 m of inset against the 3.20 m a comble sprung from the cornice would need, and the parcel is what says whether that is affordable
  · comble BUILT 3.20 m — sized by the garret storeys it holds, inside the decree's own 3.20 m allowance sprung from these eaves, and not up to the 3.90 m ceiling over them. A8.5: building to the ceiling made the roof grow by exactly what the facade declined, so the sum never moved and every building in the city reached its legal total. Nothing here reads the class — a comble is floor, not show — so the 0.70 m left under the ceiling is legal volume nobody had a use for
  · the plot: a 16.00 m parcel stands 2 whole band(s) of brisis with a room behind them — a room needs 2.00 m of floor between the two opposing slopes under 2.20 m of standing height, and on a shallow plot the slopes meet before the next band has it. This is what the cornice may not read (A15.1): the cornice runs across the party wall and parcel depths do not, so the plot limits what gets BUILT and never what was given up for it
  · comble section: a brisis of 2.90 m — 1 × 2.90 m ((a room a person lives in, plus the floor structure carrying the one above) + (the wall plate the terrasson's rafters land on, over the garret's ceiling)) — standing on the gabarit, then a terrasson at 12° closing the remaining 0.30 m over the 5.10 m back to the middle of the plot. The fold is what makes it a comble BRISÉ (A8.3)
  · comble holds a storey (1 of 1): 2.60 m clear, its floor at 16.85 m, behind band 1 of a 2.90 m brisis, inside a 3.20 m roof, with 10.80 m of floor between the slopes at its ceiling (a room needs 2.00 m — a garret room needs a bed's length of floor under full height)
  · bay pitch 2.80 m, held in [2.70, 3.40] m — the narrowest REPEATING bay a window and its two piers make sense in / the widest bay a stone lintel and the joist run behind it will span. The rhythm is what the masonry spans, so it is very nearly the same on every frontage in Paris; a comfortable builder moves it by 0.25 m and buys the rest of what the money shows in the OPENING inside the bay, in storey height and in ornament (A8.6)
  · porte_cochere: 3.40 m of frontage — the clear opening plus the jamb its head lands on either side (((SOURCED — the clear width of a porte cochère. Daly 1864 (César Daly, L'Architecture privée au XIXme siècle sous Napoléon III, Sér. 1 Vol. 1 t. 2), plan callout '2.600' at 119 avenue des Champs-Élysées, plates daly_elevation_49 / daly_detail_05 (printed dimension on the plate). The same door read off the elevation's scale bar gives 2.99 m, a 15 % error caught only because the printed value existed to check it against — which is why a printed dimension is preferred wherever one exists. Première median 2.567 m (n=4), Deuxième 2.575 m (n=3): the two classes agree to 0.4 %, so this is ABSOLUTE across the whole ladder) + (INFERRED — the jamb carrying the arch over a carriage opening; the arch's thrust does not scale with ambition, so neither does the pier under it)) + (INFERRED — the jamb carrying the arch over a carriage opening; the arch's thrust does not scale with ambition, so neither does the pier under it)). entrance placed half a bay LEFT of the axis: 1 bay(s) to its left and 2 to its right, because a run of 3 has no middle element to take. The composition answers the offset — a lone narrow special goes to the right-hand end, which is the side the door is not on
  · which is 1.05 m more frontage than a porte_pietonne would have taken — on a narrow parcel a difference that size is a whole window axis, carried up every storey. Which door a frontage has is entitlement and not ambition, so this is the one thing on the facade that buys windows or spends them (A10.2)
  · [horizontal] budget 13.0000 m
  · [horizontal] 1 fixed slot(s) reserve 3.4000 m at exactly their preferred width — absolute, so they never absorb
  · [horizontal] 3 bay(s) at preferred 2.8000 m, centreline to centreline = 8.4000 m
  · [horizontal] slack +0.5000 m
  · [horizontal] widened both ends by 0.2500 m (0.5000 m absorbed)
  · [horizontal] rung WIDEN_ENDS; residual 0.000e+00 m

role 'attic' at rank 3 from the principal floor — derived from position and height, not declared; floor level 16.848 m, storey height 2.600 m

this storey stands inside the comble — its floor at 16.848 m is the top of the stone face, not a level behind it — so nothing on the stone facade is composed on it: no opening, no surround, no keystone, no balcon filant, no cornice. What encloses it is the roof, and its windows are the lucarnes the termination phase stands on that roof, one per bay of this very storey's grid. Emitted empty rather than omitted, because it is still a floor of the building and still has the role the stack gave it.

comble inscribed in the diagonal_45 envelope: 3.200 m tall over eaves at 16.848 m — the top of the legal solid (20.750 m) reckoned from those eaves, capped by the parcel where its two slopes meet — ridge set back 8.000 m, approximated as a broken mansard of 45.0° / 12.0° breaking at 60% of its height. Nobody chose the angle — it is the boundary of the legal solid for a 18.00 m street.

dormer-and-ornament repertoire drawn from the variants genuinely in use at 1865 for a comfortable building: pedimented_dormers 100%, small_plain_dormers 39%. The comble under them is a diagonal_45 because the decree says so, which is a different kind of fact and is not on this axis

inputs.source: BRIEF.md roof: '45° comble with pedimented dormers (canonical 1853–84)'

trace.detail: the comble is a diagonal_45 because the decree in force says so, and for no other reason: geometry is a step on the decree date and carries no class lag, while 'pedimented_dormers' is fashion and does. The two are free to be out of step — a lagged builder fitting pedimented lucarnes to an arc comble is the straggler the brief calls the common case — and neither may be inferred from the other, so no variant on the fashion axis is allowed to name a comble geometry.

covering 'zinc_roofing': zinc stood at 100% prevalence at 1865 for a comfortable building, and the material axis is drawn separately from the dormer axis because a zinc roof and a pedimented dormer are not alternatives

no lucarne over bay 1 in row 1 of 1: it needs a head of 1.654 m over the eaves, but the roof surface at this bay's own centre (2.000 m along the frontage) has already fallen to 0.800 m on the hip return. A dormer built to the mid-block height here would stand clear of the tiles that are actually there, over the sky beyond the hip's own arris.

lucarne 1 lights the attic storey at index 5 (2.60 m clear, its floor at 16.85 m), and stands over that storey's horizontal slot 2 (a bay, 3.400 m wide, centred at 5.100 m), in row 1 of 1 — one row for each 2.90 m band of brisis, because each band is one room's outside wall. The count and the spacing are the storey's, not the roofscape's: a storey never lays out, it fills the one shared bay grid, so the windows in the roof line up with the windows below them by construction. End piers and inserted specials carry none.

face set back 1.654 m — exactly setback_at(1.654 m) for the diagonal_45 envelope, i.e. as far forward as the gabarit permits at the dormer's own head. Face 1.30 m (the lucarne fills the brisis of the storey it lights: a 1.90 m band of steep slope, less the 0.35 m zinc skirt below it and the 0.25 m head above it — a garret room's window is as tall as the garret's own wall) over a 0.35 m skirt (INFERRED — gutter and the first course of zinc, passing below the lucarne), standing on the band whose foot is 0.00 m over the eaves.

lucarne 2 lights the attic storey at index 5 (2.60 m clear, its floor at 16.85 m), and stands over that storey's horizontal slot 3 (a bay, 2.800 m wide, centred at 8.200 m), in row 1 of 1 — one row for each 2.90 m band of brisis, because each band is one room's outside wall. The count and the spacing are the storey's, not the roofscape's: a storey never lays out, it fills the one shared bay grid, so the windows in the roof line up with the windows below them by construction. End piers and inserted specials carry none.

Face 1.30 m (the lucarne fills the brisis of the storey it lights: a 1.90 m band of steep slope, less the 0.35 m zinc skirt below it and the 0.25 m head above it — a garret room's window is as tall as the garret's own wall) over a 0.35 m skirt (INFERRED — gutter and the first course of zinc, passing below the lucarne), standing on the band whose foot is 0.00 m over the eaves.

souche 0 on the party wall at x=0.000 m, gathering roughly 5 flue(s) — one fireplace per storey above the ground floor in the room-stack below it. The flues rise inside masonry the building already has, so the souches stand on the joints of the same bay grid as everything else. trace.detail: section through the building on a plane perpendicular to the street: pavement to eaves at 16.848 m up the facade plane, then the brisis ON the diagonal_45 envelope to the fold 1.904 m above the eaves, then the terrasson to a ridge 3.200 m above them and 8.000 m back from the facade — 4 point(s). The brisis is not chosen: it is the boundary of the legal solid, sampled, because a builder takes every centimetre of garret floor the law allows. What stands above it IS chosen — it is a roof, not an envelope (A8.3) — and it is inscribed inside the same boundary.

the fold is at 1.904 m over the eaves, 59.5% of the comble, and 1.904 m back from the facade — where the terrasson, arriving at the ridge 8.000 m back, meets the diagonal_45 envelope on its way down (A12.1). It is NOT the 2.900 m the garret's own wall stands: that number is a count of whole chambres de bonne and it puts the fold within 0.300 m of the ridge, leaving a hairline terrasson and a flat deck across the rest of the plot — a slab with a nick near the top rather than a comble brisé. The section is over-determined once the terrasson's pitch is fixed, so the SAME three numbers are read as a terrasson running the whole way to the ridge and a fold wherever that line crosses the gabarit. The ridge did not move (3.200 m, the decree's and the measured plates'); only the fold did, and it slid down the envelope, so it is still a point setback_at returned.

the comble springs from the eaves the building actually has (16.848 m, the sum of its storeys), not from the legal cornice ceiling (17.55 m) — the diagonal springs from the égout du toit, so a building that stopped short of its ceiling carries the whole roof SHAPE down with it. Its CEILING does not come down with it: 0.702 m of cornice height went unbuilt, and that is legal space the building declined to occupy rather than space it forfeited, so the SAME curve is traced to a taller top and the comble MAY stand 3.902 m over these eaves — 0.702 m more than the 3.200 m the ridge stands over the cornice — on a parcel with 8.000 m to give. The springing did not move; only the top did (A3.1). It does NOT stand there: a ceiling is not a height, and building to it made the roof grow by exactly what the stone gave up, so every immeuble in Paris came out at its legal total (A8.5). What was built is 3.200 m — the garret storeys behind the brisis and the terrasson closing over them — set back 8.000 m, leaving 0.702 m of legal volume nobody had a use for. This silhouette is inscribed below the envelope sprung from its own eaves (worst margin +0.000 m); measured from the legal cornice — the weaker line, which is not the test — it would be +0.000 m. A margin of exactly zero is the facade standing on the street line, which is where a Paris facade stands.
ends 'hipped': a corner building's comble is hipped and shows this profile at its returns; a mid-block one runs straight between party walls. Decided here so the renderer decides nothing.
